https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/reward/PhiRewards.sol#L78-L121


# Vulnerability details

In `PhiRewards::handleRewardsAndGetValueSent` can be call by anyone. The problem is  the data that is passed to be function can be anything. There are fees that are applied in this function, but if the caller pass for `addressesData_` only his addresses, all of the funds sent will be distributed to the caller, so he will not pay any fee. 

## Impact
The problem comes with that the malicious user can pass any values for chain id and art id and the backend who is monitoring for events will receive wrong data, currently this data is visualized in the fronted. 

User can DOS the system emitting a lot of events, that can be handled in the backend and can be properly visualized in the frontend. Because the database will need to persist this data.

The problem can occur on all chains, but layer 2 chains are more vulnerable, because the price of the gas is extremely low.

## Proof of Concept

Function `handleRewardsAndGetValueSent` can be call by anyone in two different ways

1. `quantity` == 0
This will enable to user to not sent any ether and the function will just emit event. For the addresses we can pass any values. And even the quantity is zero, the  contract will emit an event with wrong values. 

2. `quantity` > 0
User will need to pass ether and also for addreses which will receive rewards it will need to pass his address.

You can add this test to `Cred.t.sol` and see that event is emitted and no access controls are needed.

Add this to the beggining of `Cred.t.sol`:

```diff

+.  event RewardsDeposit(
+        bytes credData,
+        address minter,
+        address indexed receiver,
+        address indexed referral,
+        address indexed verifier,
+        bytes rewardsData
+    );

```

And add the test: 

```solidity

function test_emit_event() public {
        bytes memory addressesData_ = abi.encode(anyone, anyone, anyone, anyone);
        bytes memory rewardsData = abi.encode(0, 0, 0, 0);
        bytes memory credData = abi.encode(2, 20, false);
        vm.expectEmit();
        emit RewardsDeposit(credData, anyone, anyone, anyone, anyone, rewardsData);

        phiRewards.handleRewardsAndGetValueSent(2, 20, 0, 100, addressesData_, false);
    }
```

The test is passing and as you can see the malicious user can send any data and float the system with dummy events.

Consider making the function `handleRewardsAndGetValueSent` having access controls. 

One proposal is having a mapping in the `PhiFactory` which tracks a `PhiNft1155` created by the factory. And this functions can be called only by `PhiNft1155` created by `PhiFactory`

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/Cred.sol#L232-L280
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/Cred.sol#L283-L310
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/PhiFactory.sol#L196-L213
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/PhiFactory.sol#L215-L257
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/abstract/RewardControl.sol#L100


# Vulnerability details

In the current implementation of the protocol on many places ares used signatures. The problem is that they are not protected against replay attack due to missing nonce and chainId. We need also a chainId, because the protocol will be deployed on multiple chains, and this can lead to severe problems. This problem can be found on several places: 

1. `Cred::createCred`
2. `Cred::updateCred`
3. `PhiFactory::signatureClaim`
4. `PhiFactory::createArt`
5. `RewardControl::withdrawWithSig`

## Impact

The lack of protection against replay attacks in the use of signatures within the protocol can lead to significant security vulnerabilities. Specifically, the absence of a `nonce` and `chainId` in the signature verification process allows malicious actors to reuse previously valid signatures across different transactions or even on different chains. 

Also it's important to be mentioned that the protocol will be deployed on multiple chains and `chainId` check is must! 

1. `Cred::createCred`
One user can create mutltiple Creds on the same chain with the same signature until the signature expiration. Also it's possible to be replyed on other chains by users who has the same address.  

2. `Cred::updateCred`
One user can create mutltiple Creds on the same chain with the same signature until the signature expiration. Also it's possible to be replyed on other chains. 

3. `PhiFactory::signatureClaim`
Anyone can reply this on any chain, and some of the parameters are not signed such as `quantity`, `tokenId` and `imageUri`. Minter could sign as much as tokens as he wants.

4. `PhiFactory::createArt`
Anyone can reply this on any chain, and some of the parameters are not signed.

5. `RewardControl::withdrawWithSig`
Anyone can reply this withdraw on every other chain. We need to add `chainId` here

## Proof of Concept

We will go through all of the methods that are vulnerable to this problem:

1. `Cred::createCred`

As we can see below only the expire timestamp is validated. I will suggest to add nonce which is increasing after every transaction and also a check does the `chainId` where this is executed is the same as the chain for which this signature is signed.

```solidity
function createCred(
        address creator_,
        bytes calldata signedData_,
        bytes calldata signature_,
        uint16 buyShareRoyalty_,
        uint16 sellShareRoyalty_
    )
        public
        payable
        whenNotPaused
    {
        if (_recoverSigner(keccak256(signedData_), signature_) != phiSignerAddress) revert AddressNotSigned();
        (
            uint256 expiresIn,
            address sender,
            ,
            address bondingCurve,
            string memory credURL,
            string memory credType,
            string memory verificationType,
            bytes32 merkleRoot_
        ) = abi.decode(signedData_, (uint256, address, uint256, address, string, string, string, bytes32));
        if (expiresIn <= block.timestamp) revert SignatureExpired();
```

2. `Cred::updateCred`

Here as we can see, the problem is similar to the above one. We need to add both parameters `nonce` and `chainId` to the signature.

```solidity
function updateCred(
        bytes calldata signedData_,
        bytes calldata signature_,
        uint16 buyShareRoyalty_,
        uint16 sellShareRoyalty_
    )
        external
        whenNotPaused
    {
        if (_recoverSigner(keccak256(signedData_), signature_) != phiSignerAddress) revert AddressNotSigned();
        (uint256 expiresIn_, address sender,, uint256 credId, string memory credURL) =
            abi.decode(signedData_, (uint256, address, uint256, uint256, string));
        if (expiresIn_ <= block.timestamp) revert SignatureExpired();
```

3. `PhiFactory::signatureClaim`

Same as above, here we need to add both nonce and chainId and validate them. 

```solidity
function signatureClaim(
        bytes calldata signature_,
        bytes calldata encodeData_,
        MintArgs calldata mintArgs_
    )
        external
        payable
        whenNotPaused
    {
        (uint256 expiresIn_, address minter_, address ref_, address verifier_, uint256 artId_,, bytes32 data_) =
            abi.decode(encodeData_, (uint256, address, address, address, uint256, uint256, bytes32));

        if (expiresIn_ <= block.timestamp) revert SignatureExpired();
        if (_recoverSigner(keccak256(encodeData_), signature_) != phiSignerAddress) revert AddressNotSigned();
```

4. `PhiFactory::createArt`

Here we need to add both nonce and chain id, otherwise this could be replayed on different chains.
```solidity
function createArt(
        bytes calldata signedData_,
        bytes calldata signature_,
        CreateConfig memory createConfig_
    )
        external
        payable
        nonReentrant
        whenNotPaused
        returns (address)
    {
        _validateArtCreationSignature(signedData_, signature_); 

function _validateArtCreationSignature(bytes calldata signedData_, bytes calldata signature_) private view {
        if (_recoverSigner(keccak256(signedData_), signature_) != phiSignerAddress) revert AddressNotSigned();
        (uint256 expiresIn_,,) = abi.decode(signedData_, (uint256, string, bytes));
        if (expiresIn_ <= block.timestamp) revert SignatureExpired();
    }
```

5. `RewardControl::withdrawWithSig`

This method is using nonce, but still needs to add `chainId`.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add nonce and chain id to prevent replay attacks. 


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/Cred.sol#L641-L644


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `Cred` contract does not provide reentrancy protection and does not follow the CEI pattern, resulting in a situation where a user can reenter the contract before state changes take effect.

1. In `_handleTrade` the user gets a refund for any ether they sent over the shares price.
2. `lastTradeTimestamp[credId_][curator_]` is updated only after the refund call in `msg.sender`.
3. This allows the user to reenter and effectively bypass `SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD`
4. Impact: The user can buy any amount of shares without holding them and risking losing value (value depends on the total supply of shares and can shift during `SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD` period).
5. This allows the user to perform various "unintentional flashloan" attacks, one of which is proposed in the PoC section as an example. 
5.1. The proposed PoC strategy focuses on the attacker making a profit, but he can act destructively and deprive others of all rewards, despite losing money himself (by buying all available shares, claiming reward, and then selling them).

## Proof of Concept

The PoC is quite long, so I've posted it as a secret gist:
[High01PhiPoC.sol](https://gist.github.com/PFAhard/7b23d449c519c55b69b461142a071457)

Most of the PoC is just setup and helpers to run complex protocol functions.

The main "entry point" of the PoC is the `test_Reentrancy` function.

`test_Reentrancy` go through:
1. It creates a cred with 500 as a buy/sell fee
2. It buys another 9 shares for some user, just to make the setup more realistic (10 shares currently in total)
3. It creates art with the cred ID from the first step and the chain ID of the current chain
4. It claims 100 pieces of art, again to simulate the protocol and so that the reward is not zero
5. The attacker contract then runs his helper to:
    1. Buy 4 shares
    2. Distribute the reward to the curators
    3. Withdraw the curator reward
    4. Sell 4 shares at the same price (actually minus the fee)

The attacker's profit and, accordingly, the cost of the attack are limited by 4 factors:
1. Amount of arts minted since last distribution - high direct impact on attacker's profit
2. Amount of shares held by others - very small invert impact (more shares held by others, less profit for attacker)
3. Protocol fee - medium  invert impact (higher fee - lower profit)
4. Creator fee - medium  invert impact (higher fee - lower profit)

I tried to display this relationship on a graph, where X is `amount of shares to buy` * 10^18 and Y is profit in Ethers. The vertical line shows the optimal number of shares to buy.
[Desmos Graph](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/wumgoprvef)
![ProfitForReenter](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8ba870bd-fdfc-4a55-b714-bfebc42fce0a)


For the PoC, a realistic setup was chosen with 100 minted art, 500 for protocol and creator fees, and 10 total shares before the attacker enters.

For this setup, we need to buy 4 shares (both 3 and 5 will give a smaller profit).

For this setup, the attacker's profit is `0.000468739993385027 ether`

If the attacker waits for `SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD`, he risks losing the value of 4 shares (if other users sell their shares, the value of the attacker's shares will fall).

But since he sells them in the same block where he buys them, he does not risk any value and makes a pure profit.

## Logs for PoC

```javascript
Logs:
  110033000000000000000
  Balance before buy 0.005475501464953797 in ethers
  Attacker address: 0x3B7FC06907aC243C9dc6dD316ac1b304c3F27BB6
  Reenter
  Balance after buy 0.000000000000000001 in ethers
  Addresses to distribute 0x543076C809278c1E746312b3aEaA0E5886B3fDB3 and share 1
  Addresses to distribute 0x7FA9385bE102ac3EAc297483Dd6233D62b3e1496 and share 9
  Addresses to distribute 0x3B7FC06907aC243C9dc6dD316ac1b304c3F27BB6 and share 4
  Balance after distribute 0.000050000000000002 in ethers
  Balance after withdraw 0.001464285714285716 in ethers
  Balance after reenter 0.005944241458338824 in ethers
  Profit 0.000468739993385027 ether
```


## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Introduce `nonReentrant` modifier or update state before calling arbitrary address


## Assessed type

Reentrancy

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/reward/CuratorRewardsDistributor.sol#L87

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/reward/CuratorRewardsDistributor.sol#L106
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/reward/CuratorRewardsDistributor.sol#L107


# Vulnerability details

This loop iterates over the distributeAddresses array and calls credContract.getShareNumber for each address. If the credContract.getShareNumber function is expensive or can be manipulated to consume a lot of gas, a malicious actor could provide a large number of addresses in the distributeAddresses array to intentionally increase the gas cost of the transaction. This could make it prohibitively expensive for honest users to execute the distribute function, effectively preventing them from using the contract.

Vulnerability Details
Unbounded Loop in distributeAddresses: The code iterates over the distributeAddresses array twice:

First Loop: Aggregates the total number of shares each address holds.
Second Loop: Calculates individual rewards and prepares the data for distribution.
Since the distributeAddresses array is populated from an external call to credContract.getCuratorAddresses(), the size of this array can be arbitrarily large. If an attacker (or a natural scenario with many curators) causes this array to be extremely large, the gas required to execute this function can exceed the block gas limit.

Exploit Scenario
An attacker adds a large number of curator addresses to a specific credId by exploiting the credContract.
The attacker or any user tries to call the distribute function.
Due to the large number of addresses in the distributeAddresses array, the loop exceeds the block gas limit, causing the transaction to revert.
This results in a denial of service, where rewards cannot be distributed, effectively locking the funds in the contract.

To mitigate this vulnerability, you can introduce a maximum loop iteration limit:


uint256 maxIterations = 100; // Adjust this value as needed

for (uint256 i = 0; i < distributeAddresses.length && i < maxIterations; i++) {
    // ...
}

This will ensure that the loop terminates after a certain number of iterations, preventing unbounded gas consumption. However, it's important to set the maxIterations value carefully to avoid limiting legitimate use cases.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/Cred.sol#L247


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details

In `Cred.sol`'s `createCred` function:
```solidity
  function createCred(
      address creator_,
      bytes calldata signedData_,
      bytes calldata signature_,
      uint16 buyShareRoyalty_,
      uint16 sellShareRoyalty_
  )
      public
      payable
      whenNotPaused
  {
      if (_recoverSigner(keccak256(signedData_), signature_) != phiSignerAddress) revert AddressNotSigned();
      (
          uint256 expiresIn,
          address sender,
@>        ,
          address bondingCurve,
          string memory credURL,
          string memory credType,
          string memory verificationType,
          bytes32 merkleRoot_
      ) = abi.decode(signedData_, (uint256, address, uint256, address, string, string, string, bytes32));
      ....
      ....
  }
```

In the function `createCred`, the `credChainId` (which is the argument denoted by the line "`@>`") is ignored and not checked whether this current chain(`block.chainid`) is the same chain as the chain which was given approval by `phiSignerAddress`.

Hence, this gives malicious users the opportunity to just re-use signatures that they managed to get approval for on a different chain and use it on this current chain without permission instead.

## Proof Of Concept

**Possible sequence of exploit:**

1. `Alice` gets approval through a signed signature to deploy a cred on `Chain X`.
2. She goes to `Chain Y` where this protocol is also deployed to call `createCred` with the same signature.
3. Since, as shown above `createCred` does not check whether this current chain is the same chain as which the signature is valid for, `Alice` ends up having permission to deploy this cred on `Chain Y` even though `phiSignerAddress` only wants `Alice` to deploy it on `Chain X`.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
```diff

      address creator_,
      bytes calldata signedData_,
      bytes calldata signature_,
      uint16 buyShareRoyalty_,
      uint16 sellShareRoyalty_
  )
      public
      payable
      whenNotPaused
  {
      if (_recoverSigner(keccak256(signedData_), signature_) != phiSignerAddress) revert AddressNotSigned();
      (
          uint256 expiresIn,
          address sender,
-         ,
+         uint256 credChainId,
          address bondingCurve,
          string memory credURL,
          string memory credType,
          string memory verificationType,
          bytes32 merkleRoot_
      ) = abi.decode(signedData_, (uint256, address, uint256, address, string, string, string, bytes32));
+     require(credChainId == block.chainid, "Signature not valid for this chain");
      ....
      ....
  }  
```

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/Cred.sol#L186-L189


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerbility Details

In `Cred.sol`'s `buyShareCredFor` function:
```solidity
function buyShareCredFor(uint256 credId_, uint256 amount_, address curator_, uint256 maxPrice_) public payable {
    if (curator_ == address(0)) revert InvalidAddressZero();
    _handleTrade(credId_, amount_, true, curator_, maxPrice_);
}
```

The function only checks whether `curator_` (which is the account that `msg.sender` is buying the share for) is equals to `address(0)`. It does not check whether `curator_` has given permission to `msg.sender` or whatsoever. 

Hence the attacker can buy 1 share for the victim in order to lock their shares for `SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD`=`10 minutes`. 

Which leads to the following 2 senarios that the attacker can exploit to affect the victim and manipulate the market price of the share due to low float (`MAX_SUPPLY` only `999`).

## Senario 1 (Market manipulation while letting the victim take on unnecessary risk):

1. Suppose `Alice` is a big shareholder of a cred.
2. `Alice` no longer believes in that particular cred's popularity and wants to sell her shares.
3. Attacker `Bob` (who is also a shareholder) on the other hand is extremely bullish on the price of the shares in the next `10 minutes` (which he could have came into conclusion through either monitoring the mempool for buy orders or having knowledge about an upcoming social publicity of the cred)
4. Attacker `Bob` frontruns `Alice`'s sell order, with a `buyShareCredFor` order for `curator_ = Alice`, with 1 share.
5. After `Bob` buys 1 share for `Alice`, `Alice`'s `lastTradeTimestamp` will be updated to `block.timestamp` and `Alice`'s sell orders (or any other sell orders that she send within the next `SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD` duration) will revert resulting in her shares being temporarily locked.
6. Suppose `Bob` is right, and many buyers came along to buy shares of the cred, raising the price siginificantly due to the rather quadratic nature of the bonding curve.
7. Right before `SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD` ends, `Bob` can then sell his own shares before `Alice`'s shares unlock.
<hr/>

Note that operation 7 is **different** from simply frontrunning `Alice`'s sale of her shares as `Bob` is able to both benefit from the desperate buyers pushing the share price up during the `SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD` as well as being able to sell before big shareholder `Alice`.

Whereas if this bug did not exist, `Bob` would not be able to benefit from the price caused by both events, but rather will have to <ins>choose between **either**</ins>
* Frontrunning big shareholder `Alice` to sell before she pushes down the price of the shares through selling. (`Bob` will not be unable to benefit from the buyers buying since this happens **before** the buying)
* <ins>**Or**</ins> Letting `Alice` sell first, hold his shares, and bet on the fact that buyers will push the price of the shares back higher.

Given the quadratic nature of the bonding curve, being able to benefit from both events will bring about quite a significant profit for `Bob` and will outweigh the cost needed by him to buy 1 share for `Alice`.

This senario is also unfair to the buyers buying as `Alice` has already intended to sell her shares, and now `Bob` has successfully carried out market manipulation and took advantage of desperate buyers who are willing to buy at a higher price.

<ins>**Impact for Alice includes:**</ins>
1. Although she is able to benefit from buyers pushing the share price up, `Bob` selling near the end of `Alice`'s `SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD` means `Alice` is helpless against how much `Bob` can dump the shares during `SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD`.
2. If `Bob` is wrong about this bullish bet, and the share price crashes, `Alice` will lose alot of money which is unfair to `Alice` as she never intended to activate `SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD` on her own will but rather it was `Bob` who activated her lock period maliciously to carry out his bullish bet on the share price.

Hence, this senario has shown how `Bob` forces `Alice` to participate in this bullish bet of his, beyond her will, risking her money.

## Senario 2 (Griefing Attacks):

1. `Alice` is a big shareholder and `Bob` hates `Alice`.
2. Something bearish happens to the cred and now everyone is rushing to sell their shares of the cred as the price starts to crash.
3. `Bob` frontruns `Alice`'s intended sale with a `buyShareCredFor` with `curator_` set to `Alice` to buy her 1 share.
4. Now, her `lastTradeTimestamp` gets updated, and her shares are locked for `SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD` causing her sale and any of her future transaction within `SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD` to revert.
5. The share price crashes rapidly (due to the quadratic nature of the bonding curve)
6. At the end of `SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD`, `Alice` is left with shares at a price quadratically lower than before. Resulting in significant losses.

## Proof Of Concept
Add this function to `test/Cred.t.sol`:
```solidity
function test_shareLockBug() public {
  _createCred("BASIC", "SIGNATURE", 0x0);

  address Alice = address(0x123);
  address Bob = address(0x987);
  vm.deal(Alice, 10 ether);
  vm.deal(Bob, 10 ether);

  uint256 buyPrice = bondingCurve.getBuyPriceAfterFee(1, 1, 100);//credid,supply,amount
  vm.prank(Alice);
  cred.buyShareCred{ value: buyPrice }(1, 100, 0); //Alice becomes shareholder

  buyPrice = bondingCurve.getBuyPriceAfterFee(1, 101, 50);//credid,supply,amount
  vm.prank(Bob);
  cred.buyShareCred{ value: buyPrice }(1, 50, 0); //Bob becomes shareholder
  
  skip(2 days); //After some time has passed, both Alice and Bob's shares arent locked and are free to sell

  buyPrice = bondingCurve.getBuyPriceAfterFee(1, 151, 1);//credid,supply,amount
  vm.prank(Bob);
  cred.buyShareCredFor{ value: buyPrice }(1, 1, Alice, 0);//Bob buys 1 share for Alice to lock her shares

  vm.expectRevert(abi.encodeWithSignature("ShareLockPeriodNotPassed(uint256,uint256)", block.timestamp, block.timestamp + cred.SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD()));
  vm.prank(Alice);
  cred.sellShareCred(1, 100, 0); //Alice is unable to sell her shares (confirmed by the vm.expectRevert)
}
```

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Introduce a mapping:
```solidity
mapping(address curator => mapping(address buyer => bool trusted)) public trusted_buyer;
```
As well as a approval function where shareholders can give approval to their other trusted accounts to buy shares under their name.

Then, in `buyShareCredFor`, `trusted_buyer[curator_][msg.sender] == true` can be checked.

## Tools Used
Manual Review, Foundry, VSCode




## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/curve/BondingCurve.sol#L47-L49


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
1. Overflow Risk:
 - There's a potential for overflow in the calculation (supply_ + amount_) * 1 ether. If supply_ and amount_ are large enough, this multiplication could overflow.
2. Precision Loss:
 - The function multiplies by 1 ether (10^18) before calling _curve(), which could lead to precision loss for very small values of supply_ or amount_.
3. Negative Price:
 - It's possible for this function to return a negative value if _curve(supply_ * 1 ether) is greater than _curve((supply_ + amount_) * 1 ether), which could lead to unexpected behavior.
4. Dependency on _curve():
 - The function relies heavily on the _curve() function, which we've already identified as having potential issues (division by zero, overflow, underflow).
5. No Input Validation:
 - There are no checks on the input parameters supply_ and amount_. This could lead to unexpected results or reverts if invalid values are provided.
6. Gas Inefficiency:
 - The function calls _curve() twice, which could be gas inefficient for complex curve calculations.

## Proof of Concept
    function testGetPrice() public {
        uint256 supply = 5 ether;
        uint256 amount = 1 ether;
        uint256 price = bondingCurve.getPrice(supply, amount);
        assertGt(price, 0, "Price should be greater than zero");
        //console2.log("Price for supply", supply, "and amount", amount, "is", price);
    }

## Tools Used
AI, Foundry

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
 - Add input validation for supply_ and amount_.
 - Implement overflow protection in getPrice().
 - Refactor _curve() to prevent from zero division
 - Use safe math library to prevent overflow and underflow.

Math

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The identified vulnerability allows the curator to update the credURL associated with a credential (cred) without a subsequent verification process, which could lead to the potential falsification of the entire credential.

1. Lack of Verification: After the initial verification and creation of the NFT linked to a credential, the curator has the ability to update the credURL. However, this update process does not require any re-verification by the original artist or a third party. This means that after an NFT is created and users have claimed it, the underlying data associated with the NFT can be altered without their knowledge or consent.

2. Potential for Fraud: This loophole can be exploited to falsify credentials. The original credURL verified by users can be replaced with a different URL, leading to misinformation or fraudulent claims regarding the NFT. Users who have previously claimed the NFT based on the original data could find that the cred they own now represents something different than what was originally verified.

3. Trust Erosion: The lack of a re-verification mechanism could erode trust in the platform, as users and artists may feel insecure about the integrity of the credentials associated with their NFTs.

`signatureClaim()` will verify that the `signature_` are from the `PhiSignerAddress` using the signature.

    function signatureClaim() external payable {

            bytes32 vs_,
            address ref_,
            address verifier_,
            address minter_,
            uint256 tokenId_,
            uint256 quantity_,
            uint256 expiresIn_,

            msg.data[4:], (bytes32, bytes32, address, address, address, uint256, uint256, uint256, string, bytes32)
        );
        uint256 artId = getFactoryArtId(tokenId_);
        bytes memory claimData_ = abi.encode(expiresIn_, minter_, ref_, verifier_, artId, block.chainid, data_);
        bytes memory signature = abi.encodePacked(r_, vs_);
```

## Impact

Signature replay in `Claimable.sol`

Manual Review

Recommended to add anti-replay mechanisms to `signatureClaim()` so that the signatures is verified against the sender

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/main/src/art/PhiNFT1155.sol#L41


# Vulnerability details

### Summary

The `PhiNFT1155` token is deployed and initialized by the `PhiFactory`, with the `PhiFactory` implementation stored in the `phiFactoryContract` variable:

```solidity
    IPhiFactory public phiFactoryContract;
```

However, if the `PhiFactory` contract is upgraded, the `PhiNFT1155` token will not be able to update the `phiFactoryContract` variable to point to the new implementation. This is because the `PhiNFT1155` contract lacks a function to update this variable. Consequently, any tokens deployed prior to the upgrade will continue to use the outdated factory implementation.

### Impact

Due to the current setup, tokens that were deployed using the old `PhiFactory` implementation will not benefit from improvements or fixes introduced in a new version of `PhiFactory`. This could lead to security vulnerabilities or outdated functionality persisting in deployed tokens.

### Tools Used

Manual Review

### Recommended Mitigation Steps

To address this issue, it is recommended to implement a function in the `PhiNFT1155` contract that allows the `phiFactoryContract` variable to be updated. This function should include appropriate access controls to ensure that only authorized entities can perform the update. For example:

```solidity
function updatePhiFactoryContract(address newFactory) external onlyOwner {
    phiFactoryContract = IPhiFactory(newFactory);
}
```

# Vulnerability details

Impact

The functions _addCredIdPerAddress and _removeCredIdPerAddress are declared as public, allowing any external user to call them and modify the _credIdsPerAddress mapping. This can lead to significant security issues, such as unauthorized users adding or removing credentials associated with another user's address. This could cause a loss of important credential data for users or allow malicious actors to manipulate the data for personal gain, potentially compromising the integrity of the system.

Specifically:

Unauthorized Manipulation: Malicious users can call _addCredIdPerAddress to add credentials to another user's address, potentially flooding their account with unwanted or fraudulent credentials.
    Data Tampering: Malicious users can call _removeCredIdPerAddress to remove credentials from another user's address, leading to potential data loss or denial of service.
    Integrity Risks: The ability to manipulate these mappings could disrupt the system's integrity, allowing attackers to create discrepancies between the actual ownership and the recorded data in the system.

Proof of Concept

Example Scenario:

Unauthorized Addition:
        An attacker calls _addCredIdPerAddress(12345, victimAddress) to add the credential 12345 to the victim's address.
        This could cause the victim's address to be associated with incorrect or malicious credentials.

Unauthorized Removal:
        An attacker calls _removeCredIdPerAddress(12345, victimAddress) to remove the credential 12345 from the victim's address.
        This could cause the victim to lose access to a credential they legitimately own.

Exploit Script:

solidity

// Assume attacker has access to these functions.
    
    contract Exploit {
    function exploitAdd(address target) public {
        _addCredIdPerAddress(12345, target); // Adds credential 12345 to the target's address
    }

    function exploitRemove(address target) public {
        _removeCredIdPerAddress(12345, target); // Removes credential 12345 from the target's address
    }
}

Logs/Proof:

    Logs from calling _addCredIdPerAddress and _removeCredIdPerAddress show that an unauthorized user successfully modifies another user’s credentials.

Tools Used

    Solidity Compiler
    Remix IDE or Foundry for testing and simulating the exploit.
    Etherscan or Hardhat for transaction tracing and log analysis.

Recommended Mitigation Steps

Access Control:
Implement proper access control mechanisms such as onlyOwner, onlyAuthorized, or role-based access using OpenZeppelin’s AccessControl to restrict who can call these functions.
Example:

solidity

        function _addCredIdPerAddress(uint256 credId_, address sender_) public onlyAuthorized {
            ...
        }

        function _removeCredIdPerAddress(uint256 credId_, address sender_) public onlyAuthorized {
            ...
        }

Event Logging:
        Ensure that events are emitted whenever a credential is added or removed, to provide an audit trail and help detect unauthorized actions.

Input Validation:
        Implement checks to ensure that the caller is allowed to modify the credentials for the specified address, possibly by verifying ownership or using an authorization system.

Other

The Cred contract has a vulnerability due to inconsistent pause controls in its functions, particularly in `createArt` and `updateArtSettings`. # Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `PhiNFT1155` contract, according to the protocol's logic flow, should be deployed using the `PhiFactory` (as referenced here: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/PhiFactory.sol#L631-L632) so that the `PhiFactory` has full control over it and becomes the owner of this contracе. However, the issue is that the `PhiNFT1155` contract is a proxy contract, designed with the intention of allowing upgrades. But since the `PhiFactory` lacks any wrapper function to perform upgrades, it is currently impossible to upgrade the contract.

## Proof of Concept

1. The `authorizeUpgrade` function for the `PhiNFT1155` contract is overridden so that only the owner has the ability to upgrade it, as seen here: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/art/PhiNFT1155.sol#L352.  
2. The owner of the `PhiNFT1155` contract is always the `PhiFactory` contract, as indicated here: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/PhiFactory.sol#L631-L632.  
3. However, if we examine the `PhiFactory` contract, we find that there is no function available for upgrading the `PhiNFT1155` contract, leading to the inability to upgrade `PhiNFT1155` at all.

## Tools Used
Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add a wrapper function for upgrading `PhiNFT1155`, similar to how the pause/unpause functions are implemented (as seen here: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/PhiFactory.sol#L170-L172).


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/PhiFactory.sol#L22
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/Cred.sol#L19
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/art/PhiNFT1155.sol#L21


# Vulnerability details

## Summary  
The contracts `PhiNFT1155.sol`, `Cred.sol`, and `PhiFactory.sol` lack a storage gap, which is essential for upgradeable contracts. Without this storage gap, adding new variables during contract upgrades could lead to storage slot collisions, potentially causing serious malfunctions or loss of user funds.

## Vulnerability Details  
Upgradeable contracts must include a storage gap to allow future additions of state variables without compromising storage compatibility. This storage gap ensures that new variables added in an upgraded base contract do not overwrite variables in child contracts. The contracts `PhiNFT1155.sol`, `Cred.sol`, and `PhiFactory.sol` do not have such a storage gap, making them vulnerable to storage slot collisions during upgrades.

Without a storage gap:
- **Variable Overwrite**: New variables added to the base contract during an upgrade might overwrite existing variables in child contracts.
- **Potential Malfunction**: Overwritten variables could cause contracts to behave unexpectedly, leading to contract malfunctions.


## Impact  
The absence of a storage gap in these contracts could lead to storage slot collisions during future upgrades, causing unintended overwriting of variables. This could lead to the malfunctioning of the contracts.

## Tools Used  
- Manual code review
- OpenZeppelin documentation

## Recommendations  
1. **Introduce a Storage Gap**: Add a storage gap in each of the contracts (`PhiNFT1155.sol`, `Cred.sol`, `PhiFactory.sol`) by including a reserved space using an array or a fixed-size buffer. This will allow for the safe addition of new state variables in future upgrades without risking storage collisions.

Example:
   ```solidity
   uint256[50] private __gap;
   ```




## Assessed type

Upgradable

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `createCred`function in the Cred contract and `CreateArt` are marked as payable, allowing it to receive ETH, but it doesn't actually require or handle any payments. This discrepancy between the function's ability to receive ETH and its lack of ETH handling logic can lead to several issues:

Locked Funds: Any ETH sent to this function will be locked in the contract, as there's no mechanism to retrieve or use these funds.
User Error: Users might mistakenly send ETH when creating a credential, thinking it's required, and lose their funds.
Inconsistent Design: This creates confusion about the intended behavior of the function and the overall contract design.
Potential for Unintended Behavior: Future updates or interactions with this contract might assume that the ETH sent to this function is handled in some way, leading to bugs or vulnerabilities.
Gas Wastage: Unnecessary gas is consumed in transactions that send ETH to this function, as the ETH transfer is processed but not used.

While this issue doesn't present an immediate security risk in terms of fund theft or contract manipulation, it represents a significant design flaw that could lead to loss of user funds and confusion about the contract's functionality.

## Proof of Concept
```cred.createCred{value: 1 ether}(
    creator,
    signedData,
    signature,
    signalRoyalty,
    unSignalRoyalty
);```
A user can call this and it'll succeed

## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Remove the payable keyword if no payment is required.

If you send Ether to an address controlled by a malicious user (e.g during the refund process) before performing the action of sending `mintProtocolFee` to its destination. If the refund process is executed first the fallback funcion can immediately callback into the vulnerable function `signatureClaim` opening a window for re-entrancy.

## Proof of Concept
Here is a simplified sequence of how the attacker can execute the attack
Step 1: The attacker calls the `signaturClaim()` with crafted parameters
Step 2: The function sends a refund to the attackers address
Step 3: The attacker fallback's function is triggered during the refund transfer and immediately calls back into `signatureClaim()`
Step 4: The re-entrant call occurs before the original completion of the `signatureClaim()`(transfer of the minted protocol fee)
Step 5: The attacker can manipulate this state change to their advantage

If you send Ether to a malicious user before doing any other critical operations like sending Ether to a trusted entity to provide a chance for re-entrancy 

## Tools Used
Manual Review

Use Re-entrancy Guard on the `signatureClaim()` and `merkleClaim()`

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/reward/CuratorRewardsDistributor.sol#L77-L130


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The function `distribute` doesn't implement any access control modifier allowing anyone to be able to call this function. A malicious user can call this function targeting a `credId` with a small `totalBalance` compared to a very large `totalnum` value therefore receiving very large amount as the difference between `distributeAmount` and `actualDistributeAmount`

## Proof of Concept
Lets carefully observe the `distribute()` and see how this vulnerability can play out 
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/8c0985f7a10b231f916a51af5d506dd6b0c54120/src/reward/CuratorRewardsDistributor.sol#L77C1-L131
The specified link shows the logic implementation of the `distribute()`, as stated earlier the function doesn't use any access control modifier. However, it made some calls to certain function in the credContract; `getCuratorAddresses()` and `getShareNumber()`. observing below the code snippet for this two functions

```javascript
 /// @param credId_ The ID of the cred.
    /// @param start_ The starting index for pagination.
    /// @param stop_ The stopping index for pagination.
    /// @return The addresses that have the cred.
    function getCuratorAddresses(
        uint256 credId_,
        uint256 start_,
        uint256 stop_
    )
        public
        view
        returns (address[] memory)
    {
        CuratorData[] memory curatorData = _getCuratorData(credId_, start_, stop_);
        address[] memory result = new address[](curatorData.length);

        for (uint256 i = 0; i < curatorData.length; i++) {
            result[i] = curatorData[i].curator;
        }

        return result;
    }


 /// @notice Gets the number of share an address has for a cred.
    /// @param credId_ The ID of the cred.
    /// @param curator_ The address to check.
    /// @return The number of shares the address has for the cred.
    function getShareNumber(uint256 credId_, address curator_) external view returns (uint256) {
        return shareBalance[credId_].get(curator_);
    }

``` 

It can be seen that the `getCuratorsAddresses` also doesn't uses a access control modifier but return curator addresses related to the credId. This return value from the `getCuratorsAddresses()` which in turn is passed into the `getShareNumber()` as a parameter called `distributeAddresses`. 

This logic flow allows anyone one to be able to call this function with a valid credId, the user can further exploit the function to steal funds following the detailed explanation discussed below

Step 1: The malicious user finds an exploitable credId(small `totalBalance` compared to a very large `totalNum`)
Step 2: Calls `distribute()`
Step 3: Function performs calculation that leads to large rounding errors
Step 4: Due to this error the `actualDistributeAmount` is very much smaller than `dustributeAmount`, and the difference which is most likely the `distributeAmount` is sent to the malicious user

The malicious user gain ETH based on the discrepancy created by the rounding error successfully exploiting the contract function.

Example scenario 
Example Parameters:
totalBalance = 150 tokens
totalNum = 10,000 (total number of shares)
withdrawRoyalty = 100 (representing 1% in basis points)
RATIO_BASE = 10,000 (standard base for percentage calculation)
Step-by-Step Calculation:
Calculate the Royalty Fee:

royaltyfee = (totalBalance * withdrawRoyalty) / RATIO_BASE

Substituting the values: We have,

royaltyFee = (150 * 100) / 10_000 = 1.5


Since Solidity uses integer arithmetic, the result is rounded down, so royaltyfee equals 1 token.

Calculate the Distribute Amount:

distributeAmount = totalBalance − royaltyfee
Substituting the values: We have,

distributeAmount = 150 - 1 = 149 
Initialize Variables for Distribution:

Initialize amounts as an array to store the calculated rewards for each address, and reasons to store reasons associated with each distribution.
Initialize actualDistributeAmount to 0 to accumulate the total distributed amount.
Distribute Tokens Among Addresses:

Assume distributeAddresses.length = 3 and the shares (userAmounts) for each address are:
Address 1: 1 share
Address 2: 1 share
Address 3: 1 share
The total number of shares (totalNum) is 10,000.
For each address, the function calculates their reward:

Address 1:

userRewards1 = (distributeAmount * userAmounts1) / totalNum
userRewards1 = (149 * 1) / 10,000 = 0.0149
Since Solidity rounds down, userRewards will be 0 tokens.

This same calculation result is applicable to userRewards2 and userRewars3 since they have the same number of share

Since each reward is 0 due to rounding, the actualDistributeAmount becomes:

actualDistributeAmount=0 + 0 + 0 = 0
Balance Update:

The function updates the balance of the credId:

balanceOf[credId] =− totalBalance
Assuming the initial balance was 150, it now becomes 0.

ETH Transfer:

The ETH transfer statement:

_msgSender().safeTransferETH(royaltyfee + distributeAmount − actualDistributeAmount)
Substituting the values:

_msgSender().safeTransferETH(1 +149 − 0) = 150
Therefore, 150 tokens worth of ETH is transferred back to the sender to compensate for the rounding difference.

And in this case the sender is the malicious actor, therefore stealing the funds

## Tools Used
Manual Review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use Access control to allow only curators to be able to call the function and also ensure check to make sure the curator corresponds to the specified credId.
Also you can declared a constant e.g WAD = 10**18 and implement it in the function calculation to handle precision better


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/main/src/PhiFactory.sol#L69
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/main/src/PhiFactory.sol#L632

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The encoding of string or bytes does not apply padding at the end, unless it is part of an array or struct (then it is padded to a multiple of 32 bytes).
In general, the encoding is ambiguous as soon as there are two dynamically-sized elements, because of the missing length field.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/main/src/PhiFactory.sol#L69
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/main/src/PhiFactory.sol#L632
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/main/src/PhiFactory.sol#L765

If you use keccak256(abi.encodePacked(a, b)) and both a and b are dynamic types, it is easy to craft collisions in the hash value by moving parts of a into b and vice-versa. More specifically, abi.encodePacked("a", "bc") == abi.encodePacked("ab", "c"). If you use abi.encodePacked for signatures, authentication or data integrity, make sure to always use the same types and check that at most one of them is dynamic. Unless there is a compelling reason, abi.encode should be preferred.

https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/v0.8.25/abi-spec.html#non-standard-packed-mode
## Tools Used

title: Re-entrancy on `claimFromFactory()` function
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/main/src/art/PhiNFT1155.sol#L298


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
OpenZeppelin's ERC1155.sol includes callback functions to manage NFTs and prevent them from getting stuck in contracts. For NFT contracts, there exist some implicit external function calls that could be neglected by developers. They include onERC1155Received function. The `onERC1155Received` function was designed to check whether the receiver contract can handle NFTs. This function is invoked in the `_mint()` of the `PhiNFT1155` contract. Due to this external function call, the reentrancy could happen without being noticed by contract developer.

According to what I said above, the malicious person can abuse the same things and write in the `onERC721Received` function of his contract to call the `claimFromFactory()` function many times in a loop.

An attacker can claim a large amount of tokens using reentrancy.

https://blocksecteam.medium.com/revest-finance-vulnerabilities-more-than-re-entrancy-1609957b742f

https://www.rareskills.io/post/where-to-find-solidity-reentrancy-attacks

## Proof of Concept

The `mint()` function is called in the `claimFromFactory()` function.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/main/src/art/PhiNFT1155.sol#L182
```
    function claimFromFactory(
        uint256 artId_,
        address minter_,
        address ref_,
        address verifier_,
        uint256 quantity_,
        bytes32 data_,
        string calldata imageURI_
    )
        external
        payable
        whenNotPaused
        onlyPhiFactory
    {
        uint256 tokenId_ = _artIdToTokenId[artId_];
        if (tokenId_ == 0) {
            revert InValdidTokenId();
        }
        mint(minter_, tokenId_, quantity_, imageURI_, data_);
```

The `mint()` function calls the `_mint()` function

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-phi/blob/main/src/art/PhiNFT1155.sol#L298
```
    function mint(
        address to_,
        uint256 tokenId_,
        uint256 quantity_,
        string calldata imageURI_,
        bytes32 data_
    )
        internal
    {
        minterData[tokenId_][to_] = data_;
        advancedTokenURI[tokenId_][to_] = imageURI_;
        if (!minted[to_]) {
            minted[to_] = true;
        }

        _mint(to_, tokenId_, quantity_, "0x00");
    }
```

POC :

1. Attacker calls the `claimFromFactory()` function.

2. Due to the lack of Reentrancy Guard adherence, the attacker re-enters the `claimFromFactory()` function in `onERC1155Received` before the initial call completes.

3. This process can be repeated, allowing the attacker to claim more than their allowed.

## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add a reentrancy guard (nonReentrant())



## Assessed type

Reentrancy
